ATC: Fixed-dose combination of dihydroartemisinin and piperaquine phosphate (P01BF05)
Aim: Assess the clinical safety of dihydroartemisinic/piperaquine in four African countries
Applications: Phase IV assessment as part of the RMP. Feasible to conduct safety monitoring of more than 10,000 patients, including electrocardiography monitoring
Conclusions: The treatment was well-tolerated. QT interval prolongation may occur in children

Aim: Assess the IR of AEs and adherence in occupationally-exposed healthcare workers and healthcare students
Applications: Effectively conduct an active safety monitoring of ARVs in resource limited settings where the SPRS and healthcare systems yield very little data
Conclusions: AE are very common and could be severe/serious in some cases. Intolerance to AE was cited as the sole reason for truncating treatment, indicating the need for effective counseling, active follow-up and AE management

ATC: Fixed-dose combination of artesunate and amodiaquine (P01BF03)
Aim: Testing CEM performance and feasibility in routine practice in malaria-endemic country
Applications: Complement limited information from RCT. Quantifying and characterizing known ADR; generating information on safety, tolerability and practical aspects
Conclusions: CEM-based system is feasible, but more research is needed to assess sustainability and conditions to make it cost-effective, including the amount and quality of data generated

Aim: Describe the user and safety profile of duloxetine in daily practice
Applications: Identification of new signals of possible new ADRs (amenorrhoea, shock-like paraesthesia, and urinary disorders)
Conclusions: The ADR profile of duloxetine as reported by patients is overall similar to the profile described in the SPC, but 3 new signals were identified and need further evaluation. Four patients experienced SADR (one was fatal)

Aim: Examine the use (identify potential misuse or inappropriate/off label use) of fentanyl as prescribed in primary care
Applications: PASS as part of the RMP requirements. Feasibility of the systematic collection of physician reports of risk factors for dependence, misuse and aberrant behaviors
Conclusions: The prevalence of at least one pre-existing risk factor for dependence was 26%, whilst the frequency of aberrant behaviors observed during treatment was 8%. Patients with aberrant behaviors had several different characteristics to patients without

Aim: Determine the incidence of adverse outcomes in hospitalized patients
Applications: Study on population frequently excluded from RCT; identification of preventive measures (lab monitoring, dose adjustment) to reduce the risk of bleeding associated with anticoagulation therapy
Conclusions: Anticoagulation among hospitalized patients with CKD was significantly associated with an increased risk of bleeding and in-hospital mortality

Aim: Estimate the crude IR of AEIs following vaccination with the nasal vaccine in children and adolescents
Applications: PASS study (European regulatory guidance on enhanced safety surveillance for seasonal influenza vaccines)
Conclusions: No significant change in reactogenicity or other apparent safety signal from the data collected has been detected

ATC: Influenza, inactivated, split virus or surface antigen (J07BB02)
Aim: Assess the safety of an H1N1 vaccine during the national vaccination campaign
Applications: PASS study advised by UK medicines agency (implemented as a commitment to authorities based on European recommendations on pharmacovigilance activities)
Conclusions: AS03-adjuvanted H1N1 pandemic vaccine showed a clinically acceptable reactogenicity and safety profile in all age and risk groups studied

ATC: Influenza, inactivated, split virus or surface antigen (J07BB02)
Aim: Establish the feasibility of rapidly monitoring the new swine flu vaccines in large patient numbers receiving or offered the vaccination
Applications: Support the UK national strategy for H1N1 vaccine pharmacovigilance program; active surveillance tool for ‘near real-time' safety monitoring with minimal additional workload for HCP staff
Conclusions: No significant safety issues were identified. The use of web-based technology was successful in reducing costs and allowing the collection of high quality data directly from patients
